The most direct comparison to this is the client filter (neutrino) runs, as these perform the exact same block and prevouts read in order to populate the filter data, and then write the data for each block. Sigs is an order of magnitude more data being written, and we are also fully executing validation, excluding ~94% of sigs (99.99% until taproot). However filter computation is non-trivial.

A milestone neutrino run on this same machine completes to block 850k in 1.91 hrs (that's the last run I have, a year old, missing some big optimizations. The current signature batching run is tracking very closely against the neutrino milestone benchmark. Passing block 500k organized and about 110GiB of signature data between ecdsa single and multisig, with 99.99% and 99.95% capture rate respectively.

The bridge now supports your full 4-table batching model first-class. At the verify boundary the four tables collapse to
two verify kinds

multisig
row is one ECDSA signature, a
threshold
(tapscript CHECKSIG / CHECKSIGADD) row is one Schnorr signature. The
m|n
group

bytes are accounting metadata carried in the opaque tail and are never interpreted by the bridge (m-of-n satisfaction stays your job, downstream of the per-row verdict).
Throughput (measured)
bench_lbtc_4table

performance

1,000,000 signatures per table

schnorr

Notes:
CPU is the
single-core mandatory reference
(the consensus anchor, always available). A node parallelizes it across cores; the figure above is per-core.
GPU figures are end-to-end for a saturating 1M batch; smaller batches pay relatively more transfer/launch overhead.
Numbers are valid only for this machine; re-measure elsewhere.
Usage

2. Multisig / threshold table — typed-span, zero-copy

std::span<const MultisigRow>  ms = ...;   // EcdsaRecord  + m|n + group + block-fk (135B)

At the verify boundary the four tables collapse to *two verify kinds*: a `multisig` row is one ECDSA signature, a `threshold` (tapscript CHECKSIG / CHECKSIGADD) row is one Schnorr signature. The `m|n` + `group` bytes are accounting metadata carried in the opaque tail and are never interpreted by the bridge (m-of-n satisfaction stays your job, downstream of the per-row verdict).
Throughput (measured)
`bench_lbtc_4table`, measured on this machine — Intel i5-14400F + NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti, `performance` governor, best-of-4, *1,000,000 signatures per table*, end-to-end (host de-interleave + H2D transfer + kernel + per-row result copy — what a node actually pays, not kernel-only).

The verify core reads only the leading record and walks `stride = record + key_size`, so the accounting tail costs nothing — measured, not inferred.

Usage

```#include "ufsecp_libbitcoin.h"
using namespace ufsecp::lbtc;

Controller ctrl;                       // AUTO: GPU if present, else CPU reference
if (!ctrl.ok()) { /* no usable backend — the only failure is reported here */ }```
*1. Single ECDSA / Schnorr table — results[]*

```// rows: n × (EcdsaRecord(129) + block-fk(3)); key_size = 3 (the opaque tail)
std::vector<uint8_t> results(n);
ctrl.verify_ecdsa(rows, n, /*key_size=*/3, results.data());   // results[i] == 1 valid / 0 invalid
ctrl.verify_schnorr(srows, n, /*key_size=*/3, results.data());```
*2. Multisig / threshold table — typed-span, zero-copy*

```// Your packed table forwards directly; key_size = sizeof(Row) - record is recovered from the type.
std::span<const MultisigRow>  ms = ...;   // EcdsaRecord  + m|n + group + block-fk (135B)
std::span<const ThresholdRow> th = ...;   // SchnorrRecord + m|n + group + block-fk (134B)
ctrl.verify_multisig (ms, r1.data());     // == ECDSA path,  key_size 6
ctrl.verify_threshold(th, r2.data());     // == Schnorr path, key_size 6```
*3. Collect — rejected-id list (no results[] array)*

ctrl.collect_multisig(batch);
for (auto& row : batch)                    // survivors = the rejected set (m|n+group+block-fk intact)
    if (tail_nonzero(row)) rejected.push_back(row);```

```struct MultisigRow  { EcdsaRecord   record; uint8_t mn; uint8_t group[2]; uint8_t block_fk[3]; }; // 135
struct ThresholdRow { SchnorrRecord record; uint8_t mn; uint8_t group[2]; uint8_t block_fk[3]; }; // 134```

Correct. With the current UF GPU verification ABI, the GPU-facing input is columnar: message hashes, public keys, and signatures are passed as separate contiguous buffers. So if the source table is stored as horizontal rows, some row-to-column transformation is currently required before calling the existing GPU path.

What I meant by “no copy” was only that the bridge does not interpret or copy the correlation tail into the verification core. That was too broad as written. The packed-row path still de-interleaves the verified record bytes into the existing columnar GPU ABI.

The clean way to avoid that bridge-side transformation is to expose both formats:
1. keep the current packed-row API for callers that naturally produce `[record | key]` rows;
2. add a columnar API for callers that can store/produce `hashes[]`, `pubkeys[]`, `sigs[]`, and optional `keys[]` directly.

Then libbitcoin can choose the storage layout. If you keep the row table, the transform is necessary for the current GPU ABI. If you produce vertical columns, the bridge can forward them directly to UF’s existing GPU calls and skip the row-to-column copy.

I agree that the multisig correlation pass itself should not be the bottleneck if it is O(n), allocation-free, and runs after per-row signature verdicts are known. The expensive part to avoid is streaming the signature records through an extra host-side de-interleave pass.

elements.text:
For a 3.5B-tuple run, the transform cost is dominated by memory traffic, not CPU arithmetic.
With the current row path, each tuple has to be read once from the horizontal table and written once into vertical buffers before UF can call the existing columnar GPU ABI.
Approximate payload per tuple:
ECDSA: 32-byte hash + 33-byte compressed pubkey + 64-byte signature = 129 bytes.
Schnorr: 32-byte hash + 32-byte x-only pubkey + 64-byte signature = 128 bytes.

If the correlation key is part of the transformed bridge record, add 6 bytes, but for vertical storage it can remain an independent libbitcoin-side column and does not need to be passed to UF verification.
So for 3.5B tuples:
ECDSA verify payload: 3.5B * 129 = ~451.5 GB decimal, ~420.5 GiB.
Schnorr verify payload: 3.5B * 128 = ~448.0 GB decimal, ~417.2 GiB.
With a 6-byte key included: add ~21.0 GB decimal, ~19.6 GiB.
A row-to-column transform touches at least read + write, so the extra memory traffic is roughly:
ECDSA: ~903 GB decimal / ~841 GiB.
Schnorr: ~896 GB decimal / ~834 GiB.
With 6-byte key copied too: add another ~42 GB decimal / ~39 GiB traffic.
Wall-clock estimate depends on sustained host memory bandwidth:
50 GB/s effective: ~18 seconds for ~900 GB.
100 GB/s effective: ~9 seconds.
150 GB/s effective: ~6 seconds.
200 GB/s effective: ~4.5 seconds.

In practice it may be worse if this is NUMA-unfriendly, competes with mmap/page-cache traffic, or runs while GPU transfers are also consuming bandwidth. It may also be partially hidden if transform is pipelined while previous chunks are on the GPU.
The main point: the transform is not asymptotically expensive, but at 3.5B tuples it is a real full-chain memory-bandwidth tax. Vertical storage avoids one full read+write pass over roughly 0.45-0.47 TB of data per validation run. If the correlation key remains an independent libbitcoin column, UF does not need to receive or copy it for pure signature verification.

elements.text:
Concrete example:

Horizontal storage today:

    row[i] = hash32 | pubkey33 | sig64 | correlation_key6

For ECDSA that is 129 bytes of verification data plus the 6-byte key. The bridge then has to de-interleave this into:

    hashes[n][32]
    pubkeys[n][33]
    sigs[n][64]

before calling the existing UF GPU verification ABI.

Vertical storage would instead keep the data as:

    hashes[]   = mmap column, n * 32 bytes
    pubkeys[]  = mmap column, n * 33 bytes for ECDSA, or n * 32 for Schnorr
    sigs[]     = mmap column, n * 64 bytes
    keys[]     = independent libbitcoin correlation column, not needed by UF verify

Then the bridge can call the column API directly:

    ufsecp_lbtc_verify_ecdsa_columns(
        ctrl,
        hashes,
        pubkeys,
        sigs,
        count,
        results);

or, if you want the collect-style behavior:

    ufsecp_lbtc_verify_ecdsa_columns_collect(
        ctrl,
        hashes,
        pubkeys,
        sigs,
        count,
        keys,
        6);

In the pure verify case UF does not need the key column at all. The key can remain fully owned by libbitcoin and used later for correlation.

Cost example for 3.5B ECDSA tuples:

    3.5B * (32 + 33 + 64) = 451.5 GB of verification payload.

A row-to-column transform must at least read that payload once and write the column buffers once:

    ~451.5 GB read + ~451.5 GB write = ~903 GB memory traffic.

At 100 GB/s sustained host memory bandwidth, that is roughly 9 seconds of extra memory-bandwidth work. At 50 GB/s it is roughly 18 seconds. If the 6-byte key is also copied, add about 42 GB more traffic, but with vertical storage the key does not need to be passed to UF verification.

So the transform is not algorithmically complex, but over a full-chain-sized 3.5B tuple run it is a real memory-bandwidth tax. If libbitcoin can produce vertical columns directly, UF can skip that pass and use the existing GPU-facing layout directly.

That sounds like the right tradeoff.

If the vertical layout is produced directly from mmap-backed physical tables, then collapsing to two logical tables (ECDSA and Schnorr) and keeping the correlation bytes in the stored row format is preferable to paying the horizontal-to-vertical transform cost. The extra ~3 unused bytes on single-signature rows is a small fixed storage overhead (~1.6% by your estimate), while avoiding the extra ~0.5TB copy/allocation over a full run is a much cleaner win.

From the engine/bridge side I would keep the interface at the column level:

- ECDSA: hashes, public keys, signatures, optional/retained correlation column
- Schnorr: hashes, public keys, signatures, optional/retained correlation column

The correlation column does not need to be passed into the core verify engine unless that specific call needs it. For normal single-sig rows it can just remain part of the caller-owned table layout and be ignored. For multisig/threshold correlation, the bridge can use the same physical format and select the correlation behavior internally.

So I agree: two logical tables backed by vertical physical tables is simpler, avoids the row transform, reduces call complexity, and keeps the wasted bytes small enough that it is not worth optimizing separately until measured otherwise.

For normal single-sig rows it can just remain part of the caller-owned table layout and be ignored. For multisig/threshold correlation, the bridge can use the same physical format and select the correlation behavior internally.

So I agree: two logical tables backed by vertical physical tables is simpler, avoids the row transform, reduces call complexity, and keeps the wasted bytes small enough that it is not worth optimizing separately until measured otherwise.

elements.text:
Think of it this way... there is a continuous flow of values into a table, and into a vector.

The table writes are concurrent by block and at the granularity of tx outputs. The vector writes are sequential (stranded) by block (input would be way too much to message-buffer, blocks is easy/slow). The vector is only submitted to the message pump after the table writes for that block are committed.

The critical section only makes write and verify/purge mutually-exclusive (and since verify is extremely rare, there is no meaningful contention).

The strand will deliver batched messages to the vector at any time, but cannot do so during verify, because both are on the same strand. So batched cannot be increased during verify, and is purged at the end of verify.

So a latent block id making its way through the message pump may land on batched
after

the table(s) that contained the records for that same block are purged. This doesn't matter. The tables only carry verification failure, so if the block failed, it's a reset.

This latent block id will land once verification completes and has purged both the tables and the batched_ vector. This is fine. The block will get marked as valid on the next verification.

The final (residual) batches ensure that both the tables and the batched_ vector are processed in full before batching gives way to non-batching.

i am glad i chased it down, tho, because i do think i have something. i kept looking at the code and something didn't sit right. so here is what i believe can happen:

imagine block
a
has a bad sig. when validating `a` the bad signature row is written into the batch table under the batch mutex. But
a

’s block id is not added to batched_ at that moment, rather it is posted later to the strand via push_batch().

before push_batch() runs, block
b
finishes and triggers batch verification. verifier sees
a
’s bad signature row, correctly marks
a
unconfirmable, and purges the table. but because
a
’s id is not yet in batched_, the invalid link cleanup cannot mark
a

’s entry as terminal.
now
a
’s delayed push_batch() finally runs and appends
a
to batched_. On the next batch, process_valids() treats every non-terminal link in batched_ as valid, so

Completed a database generalization that allows a set of mmaps (files) to be defined and configured as one set, while retaining fluent names to navigate to the individual files. So the set abstraction can hide the distinction for nearly all of the overhead, while keeping the detail is conveniently accessible.

Did the same for tables that would use the multiple file mappings. A table combines a head and body. So for a four column SoA (vertical) table there are 8 files (mmaps) as 4 heads and 4 bodies, with corresponding programmatic names and file names. The table abstraction similarly allows this to be defined and configured as one table, while retaining fluent names to navigate to the individual columns.

These changes allow 11 tables, with 22 files to be represented as 3 tables with 6 files. And if we want to split out multisig from ecdsa and schnorr, that becomes 5 tables over 10 files, vs. 19 tables over 38 files. The actual tables and files are still there, just a lot less code overhead, thanks to the magic of metaprogramming.

The vertical batch tables change seems to have significantly increased the I/O cost relative to the horizontal. The horizontal tables produced a neutral if not slightly better outcome with batched verification, despite the significant increase in writes. The net verification cost against both table types inclusive of read and post-processing cost is about the same (350K sps). And the marshalling code is identical. And perf analysis shows a general increase in store contention/paging across the spectrum (all costs increasing as they all resolve to the store (read block, read prevouts, confirmation queries, signature writes).

Full CPU validation time when batching vertical is 2x batching horizontal (9 vs. 4.5 hrs), and the latter is slightly better than no batching at all. This is significant enough that we will need to measure the benefit of potentially-optimized GPU throughput against this increased marshalling cost. Since GPU can't make up more than 4.5 hrs on 3 hrs of GPU signing cost, the above is prohibitive even with an infinite sps GPU.
